name: Bad Mergentheim Witch Trials
regional_context: Bad Mergentheim, Württemberg, Holy Roman Empire; seat of the Teutonic Order in Franconia; Protestant-Catholic mixed territory in the shadow of the larger Franconian mass persecutions
summary: The Bad Mergentheim trials (1628-1629) were a contained but lethal prosecution occurring in the orbit of the larger simultaneous Franconian panics in Bamberg and Würzburg. Mergentheim was the seat of the Teutonic Order's Deutschmeister, creating a distinctive jurisdictional context — prosecutions proceeded under Order authority rather than a prince-bishopric or free city council. Approximately 20 individuals were accused and 14 executed over two years. The trials coincided with the peak of the Franconian persecutions and show how regional panic dynamics could spread to neighboring jurisdictions through shared denunciation networks and information circulation.
historiographical_significance: Mergentheim illustrates the contagious dynamics of regional witch panics: persecution in large territories created pressure on neighboring jurisdictions to prosecute, both through shared accusatory networks (confessing witches named suspects across territorial boundaries) and through social pressure not to appear lax in a period of intense demonological anxiety. Levack's analysis of the role of regional communication networks in spreading prosecution pressure is directly applicable. The Teutonic Order context also adds an unusual institutional dimension — the Order had its own legal culture and administrative apparatus distinct from both episcopal and civic German jurisdictions.

key_details.initiating_authority: Teutonic Order Deutschmeister administration at Mergentheim
key_details.procedure: Standard German inquisitorial procedure; torture applied; denunciations exchanged with neighboring Franconian territories

trial_phases.context: Regional panic from Bamberg and Würzburg creates pressure; local accusations surface in the context of broader Franconian crisis
Approximately 14 executions; cross-jurisdictional denunciations with Bamberg/Würzburg networks
Trials conclude as regional panic begins to recede and initial suspect pool is exhausted

scholarly_disagreement: Documentation for the Mergentheim trials is relatively sparse compared to the major Franconian persecutions, making precise reconstruction difficult. Historians debate the degree to which the Mergentheim trials were independently generated by local tensions or primarily driven by external pressure and cross-jurisdictional denunciations from the larger Franconian hunts.
source_method: Teutonic Order administrative records (fragmentary); Behringer's regional studies; Württemberg archival sources
historiographical_notes: Mergentheim's marginal documentation status relative to the major Franconian persecutions is itself historically significant: smaller, less-lethal trials in the shadow of mass panics often escape detailed record because they were administratively routine rather than exceptional. This documentation bias means historians working primarily from major cases may systematically underestimate the breadth of regional persecution. The Teutonic Order's administrative distinctiveness also represents an opportunity to test whether institutional culture moderated or enabled persecution — a question that the sparse records unfortunately cannot fully answer.
